extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of The Spectator; genteel early-18th-century public interested in manners, taste, and moral reflection
extracted.subtask_short: spectator essays on manners and taste
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance and reflections on behaviour, art-judgment, virtue, and innocent amusements aimed at improving private and public taste and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a 'wise' picture
rubrics_metrics.description: A Picture that is thoroughly understood in the Whole, and well performed in the Particulars, that is begun on the Foundation of Geometry, carried on by the Rules of Perspective, Architecture, and Anatomy, and perfected by a good Harmony, a just and natural Colouring, and such Passions and Expressions of the Mind as are almost peculiar to Raphael; this is what you may justly style a wise Picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast 'wise' pictures (built on geometry, perspective, anatomy, harmony, natural colouring, expressive passions) with merely 'witty' or flashy works. A true masterwork requires study, technical foundations, and expressive truth, not merely showy colours or mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pictures that only please the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: That Picture that only pleases the Eye, without representing some well-chosen Part of Nature or other, does but shew what fine Colours are to be sold at the Colour-shop, and mocks the Works of the Creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art which is solely decorative or gaudy, without representing nature or meaningful subject, is inferior and deceptive; value should be given to representation and subject matter, not purely to superficial splendour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge art with reason and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Man when he looks on a Picture should examine it according to that share of Reason he is Master of, or he will be in Danger of making a wrong Judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent observation of nature and thoughtful reflection sharpen taste; avoid hasty judgments and let reason play a part in assessing art so as not to mistake gaudiness for greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate observation of nature to form taste
rubrics_metrics.description: If Men as they walk abroad would make more frequent Observations on those Beauties of Nature which every Moment present themselves to their View, they would be better Judges when they saw her well imitated at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively study natural beauty to correct errors of pretenders and to develop a reliable standard for judging artistic imitation and workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is naturally beautiful and lovable
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue... is of an amiable and lovely Nature. We love a virtuous Man, who lives in the remotest Parts of the Earth... one who died several Ages ago, raises a secret Fondness and Benevolence for him in our Minds, when we read his Story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat virtue as intrinsically attractive; moral qualities inspire affection and esteem across distance and time and should be valued apart from utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer virtues that benefit others for popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Those which make a Man popular and beloved, are Justice, Charity, Munificence, and, in short, all the good Qualities that render us beneficial to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While temperance and devotion are laudable, public affection is more often won by qualities that actively do good to others; even extravagant generosity can outshine more private merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerfulness and good-nature as ornaments of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great Ornaments of Virtue, which shew her in the most advantageous Views, and make her altogether lovely, are Chearfulness and Good-Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traits prevent virtue from souring into severity or melancholy; a virtuous person should cultivate ease and good humour to make their virtue attractive and socially effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let political hatreds obscure moral admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Men may oppose one another in some Particulars, but ought not to carry their Hatred to those Qualities which are of so amiable a Nature in themselves... We should esteem Virtue though in a Foe, and abhor Vice though in a Friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the distinction between political disagreement and moral judgement; recognise and respect virtue across party lines instead of using religion or faction to blacken character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper audience etiquette: avoid self-display that disturbs others
rubrics_metrics.description: This Person where-ever he came into a Room made a profound Bow... then took the Gross of the Room, by passing by them in a continued Bow... he obliged us with several Views of his Person from every Opening... this Practice must be confess'd to diminish the Pleasure of the Audience, and for that Reason presumptuous and unwarrantable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers or audience members who intrude upon the stage or repeatedly display themselves (leaping over spikes, appearing behind curtains, frequent stage interruptions) spoil others' enjoyment and are improper; such behaviour may be regulated or forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecent or licentious speech in mixed company
rubrics_metrics.description: The impertinent Observations which the Coxcomb made upon our Shame and Confusion were such, that it is an unspeakable Grief to reflect upon them... how necessary is it to repeat Invectives against such a Behaviour?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers in public or mixed company should refrain from indecent language or impertinent remarks that inflict suffering on modest persons; admonitions and social censure are appropriate remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend innocent, family-friendly pastimes
rubrics_metrics.description: I would gladly know in particular, what Notion you have of Hot-Cockles; as also whether you think that Questions and Commands, Mottoes, Similes, and Cross-Purposes have not more Mirth and Wit in them, than those publick Diversions... I would have these Sports and Pastimes not only merry but innocent, for which Reason I have not mentioned either Whisk or Lanterloo, nor indeed so much as One and Thirty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favoured domestic entertainments should be sociable, witty, and harmless (e.g. blind-man's-buff, questions and commands) rather than gambling or vice-associated games; recommend pastimes that preserve family comfort and moral propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocence needs worldly knowledge to avoid ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing which one regards so much with an Eye of Mirth and Pity as Innocence, when it has in it a Dash of Folly... I am heartily concerned when I see a virtuous Man without a competent Knowledge of the World; ... The Virtuous and the Innocent may know in Speculation what they could never arrive at by Practice, and by this Means avoid the Snares of the Crafty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage education about the ways of the world so that innocence and virtue are not easily exploited or made ridiculous; the periodical's purpose is to open readers' insight without corrupting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exempla and satire to inform without vitiation
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be any Use in these my Papers, it is this, that without presenting Vice under any false alluring Notions, they give my Reader an Insight into the Ways of Men, and represent human Nature in all its changeable Colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essays and examples should expose folly and vice realistically to educate readers, while avoiding glamorising vice; the goal is preventive insight rather than moral corruption.
